newsitem.title: USA: Fed should be more open on rate policy - economists.
newsitem.headline: Fed should be more open on rate policy - economists.

text.p: Having drawn rave reviews for telling us when they decide to raise or lower interest rates, Federal Reserve officials are now being urged to give us better clues on how they get there.

By disclosing its moves on interest rates, the central bank has helped cut borrowing costs for millions of Americans by reducing uncertainty in financial markets and thus bringing long-term interest rates down, economists said.
But more information about Fed policy could help investors even more and further help the economy, some analysts said.

"If you're walking down a dark alley, wouldn't you like to see a sign that told you there was a mugger waiting for you," said Robert Brusca, chief economist at The Nikko Securities Co. International Inc.

Pension funds, corporations and other big investors have hundreds of millions of dollars on the line every day, and any direction money managers can glean on where interest rates are headed could help them better protect their investments.
Some economists think the Fed should set a specific policy objective and tone down the background noise that they say obscures the central bank's real agenda.

The Fed technically answers to Congress, where the Senate must approve the president's appointments to the central bank's board of governors. Its charter, written by Congress, calls for maximum sustainable economic growth, low unemployment, stable prices and a stable dollar and moderate long-term interest rates.

But legislators, economists and reporters have struggled for years to interpret the deliberations at the central bank and remarks by Fed officials -- including Chairman Alan Greenspan -- often with little success.

In a typical remark before a Congressional panel last July, Greenspan summed up the economy this way, "I think we are approaching some form of a fulcrum, where the economy can go in two significantly different ways."

Or witness the contradictory headlines on July 8, 1995, after another Greenspan Congressional appearance. The New York Times reported "Greenspan Sees Chance Of Recession" while the Wall Street Journal trumpeted "Fed Chairman Doesn't See Recession on the Horizon."

"The Fed should say: This is what we are committed to do and do nothing else. Then the public would have no uncertainty as to what to expect," said Anna Schwartz, research associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research, a group that tracks the ups and downs of the economy.

The publicity-shy Fed took a big step into the public eye on Feb. 4, 1994, when it announced for the first time that it wanted to "increase slightly pressure on reserves," which Fed-watchers knew meant an increase in a key short-term rate.

Since then, the Fed has announced all 10 of its moves on interest rates, generally after regularly scheduled meetings of Fed policy-makers, allowing investors, analysts and other interested parties to prepare for any possible moves.

In addition, the Fed has added more information to the minutes of its policy-makers' meetings, released after the subsequent meeting, and started releasing full transcripts after a five-year delay, analysts noted.

"The Fed does deserve some credit. Most people would like a little more information, but you can understand why Chairman Greenspan likes to hold his cards close to the table," said William Dudley, U.S. economic director at Goldman, Sachs & Co.
"It gives him more flexibility. There is a trade-off."
Still, some critics said five years was too long to wait for the verbatim texts of the meetings of Fed policy-makers.
Former Fed Board Gov. John LaWare said earlier this year that he would support more timely release of the transcripts.
"In my opinion, there would be no disadvantage to releasing (transcipts) six months after the (rate) decision. I have never been a believer that all this secrecy was necessary," he told Reuters.
But some analysts said it was not wise to push the central bank too far. For example, recent proposals to videotape policy-makers' meetings drew little support.
"There is such a thing as too much transparency. If you open up the meetings too much, it will push the true discussions underground," said Dudley.
